book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

scenes.title: A vector is a list of numbers
scenes.claim: Vector describes the numerical object, not its meaning
scenes.narration: A search vendor says: we use vectors, not keywords. It sounds like a leap into a new universe. But keywords can be vectors too. Chapter eight reveals what those numbers actually store, and why the word vector tells you surprisingly little about a search system.

scenes.title: Give every word a coordinate
scenes.claim: Fixed vocabulary: attack · cancer · heart · interview · job · tips · treatment
scenes.narration: Start with three tiny documents: heart attack treatment, job interview tips, and cancer treatment. Arrange their seven vocabulary terms in a fixed order. Each term gets its own coordinate. Attack is always first, cancer second, heart third. The ordering can be arbitrary, but it must stay consistent.

scenes.title: Light up the words that are present
scenes.narration: Put a one where a term occurs, and zero where it does not. Now each document is a vector. Most coordinates are empty, so these vectors are sparse. In a huge vocabulary, implementations can store the active term and weight pairs, without writing out millions of zeros.

scenes.title: The coordinates do not choose the rules
scenes.claim: Overlap: D1=2, D3=1, D2=0   |   AND: D1   |   OR: D1,D3
scenes.narration: Search for heart treatment. Counting shared ones gives document one two overlaps, document three one, and document two none. But heart AND treatment admits only document one. Heart OR treatment admits one and three. Same term evidence, different rules. Binary coordinates do not secretly contain Boolean operators.

scenes.title: Presence becomes frequency
scenes.claim: D1 with treatment repeated three times: [1,0,1,0,0,0,3]
scenes.narration: What if treatment occurs three times? A binary representation still records one. Raw term frequency records three. The coordinates keep their names; only the values change. Repetition can signal what a text is about, but unlimited counts can also reward repetition and document length too heavily.

scenes.title: Rarer terms can carry stronger evidence
scenes.claim: TF–IDF: term frequency × collection rarity; exact formulas vary
scenes.narration: Term frequency looks inside a document. Inverse document frequency looks across the collection. Treatment appears in two of our documents; heart appears in just one. TF IDF gives the rarer term more collection level emphasis. It is still a sparse vector with named vocabulary coordinates.

scenes.title: BM25 changes the weights, not the vocabulary
scenes.claim: IDF + diminishing returns + document-length normalisation
scenes.narration: BM twenty five also uses rarity, but repetition brings diminishing returns, and document length adjusts the contribution. You can view its score as a sum of matching term weights. In practice, an inverted index jumps to active terms. This comparison of representations is not a historical derivation of BM twenty five.

scenes.title: A vector is not a promise of semantics
scenes.claim: Same lexical coordinates; richer weights and different retrieval rules
scenes.narration: Binary presence, term frequency, TF IDF, and BM twenty five can all be written as vectors. Their dimensions remain lexical. Richer weights do not turn them into dense semantic embeddings. Ask what the coordinates mean, where the numbers came from, and what rules use them. Next, we separate those questions.

scenes.title: Four questions, four different answers
scenes.claim: Vector?   Sparse or dense?   Specified or learnt?   What evidence?
scenes.narration: Imagine four switches on a search machine. Is the representation a vector? Are few coordinates active, or most? Was its weighting rule specified, or learnt during training? And what evidence do its dimensions preserve? These are separate questions. One shiny product label cannot answer them all.

scenes.title: Sparse and dense describe shape
scenes.claim: Few active coordinates versus mostly active coordinates; toy values
scenes.narration: A sparse vocabulary vector might have millions of possible coordinates and only a few hundred active ones. A dense embedding is often much shorter, with most coordinates active. Neither shape tells you whether the representation is good, whether it was trained, or what its numbers mean.

scenes.title: A latent coordinate has no single word label
scenes.claim: Toy dense vector: latent 3 = 0.81 does not mean citation
scenes.narration: In a lexical vector, a coordinate can carry a name like citation. A dense text embedding instead uses learnt latent dimensions. Their contribution is distributed across the representation. Our illustrative third coordinate, zero point eight one, does not mean citation by itself. These numbers are not measured model output.

scenes.title: Dense does not automatically mean semantic
scenes.claim: [year, pages, references, citations] = [2026,14,32,87]
scenes.narration: Here is a counterexample hiding in plain sight: year, pages, references, and citations. All four values are nonzero, so this bibliographic feature vector is dense. It records explicit facts about an article. Its density alone does not make it a semantic text embedding.

scenes.title: Sparse does not automatically mean untrained
scenes.claim: BM25: specified formula   |   SPLADE: learnt vocabulary weights
scenes.narration: Now turn the assumption around. A sparse representation can be learnt. SPLADE predicts weights over a language model's output vocabulary, while a sparsity constraint encourages almost all entries to stay zero. Its vocabulary is typically WordPiece subword units, rather than the analysed terms in an ordinary lexical index.

scenes.title: Words absent from the input can receive weight
scenes.claim: Schematic expansion; whole words and weights are illustrative
scenes.narration: Read heart attack. A learnt sparse representation might also activate myocardial and infarction, even if they never appeared in the input. The model predicts weights instead of merely counting words. Our whole word labels and weights are schematic. A real model activates entries in its own vocabulary, and expansion depends on training.

scenes.title: Separate density from the source of the weights
scenes.claim: BM25: sparse + specified   |   SPLADE: sparse + learnt   |   bi-encoder: dense + learnt
scenes.narration: Place the methods on two independent axes. BM twenty five is sparse with a specified formula. SPLADE is sparse with a learnt mapping. A dense bi encoder is dense with a learnt mapping. Named sparse coordinates can support meaning aware expansion. Density alone predicts none of those distinctions.

scenes.title: The comparison rule is another choice
scenes.claim: Representation → comparison score → retrieval rule
scenes.narration: Even the arithmetic is a separate decision. Dot product can compare sparse vocabulary weights or dense features. Cosine can compare different numerical representations too. Neither operation makes a vector semantic. The representation supplies evidence, the comparison supplies a score, and the retrieval rule decides how that score is used.

episodes.title: What does it mean to search a paper?
episodes.subtitle: Documents, chunks, vectors, and results

scenes.title: One paper can become many searchable items
scenes.claim: Source document ≠ indexed unit ≠ representation ≠ displayed result
scenes.narration: You see a paper in a result list. Did the search system compare the whole article, its abstract, or a tiny passage? Those choices are hidden behind the same familiar card. Chapter eight separates the source document, the indexed unit, its representation, and the result you actually see.

scenes.title: Choose how finely to cut the source
scenes.claim: One article → one abstract, ten sections, or fifty overlapping passages
scenes.narration: Imagine a twenty page article. A system might index one abstract, ten sections, or fifty overlapping passages. Those passages are chunks: the text units searched at that stage. The source is still one article. Changing the cut changes which local evidence can compete for a match.

scenes.title: Many chunks, many independent representations
scenes.claim: Conventional single-vector bi-encoder: one pooled vector per indexed unit
scenes.narration: In a conventional single vector bi encoder, each indexed unit receives one pooled vector. Fifty passages become fifty independently searchable vectors. That does not mean one vector captures the complete paper. Nor does it mean the system automatically combines evidence scattered across the separate passages.

scenes.title: A boundary can separate the clue from its context
scenes.claim: Chunk size and overlap change what is represented together
scenes.narration: A chunk boundary can separate a finding from a qualification, or a method from the population it studied. Overlapping windows can preserve some neighbouring text, but no cut guarantees perfect context. The size, overlap, and encoding of the units all affect what evidence the retrieval stage sees together.

scenes.title: Four matching chunks can become two papers
scenes.claim: A2 + A7 + A9 → Paper A   |   B3 → Paper B; grouping is not score fusion
scenes.narration: Suppose retrieval finds passage two, seven, and nine from paper A, plus passage three from paper B. That is four chunks from two papers. The interface may group them by source identity. Grouping alone does not specify how scores are combined, or combine their evidence into an answer.

scenes.title: An abstract index cannot directly match unseen results
scenes.claim: What is indexed limits what can match at that retrieval stage
scenes.narration: If only the abstract was indexed, a claim found only in the results section cannot directly match that stage. Full text passages make different evidence reachable. A product saying it searches articles does not settle this question. Establish the actual searchable text, and the granularity of each unit.

scenes.title: Retrieved text and answer context can differ
scenes.claim: Indexed text → retrieved unit → later fetch or expansion → generator context
scenes.narration: But retrieval is not always the end of the story. A later step may fetch full text, neighbouring passages, or a parent section. It may also compress several retrieved units before assembling an answer model's context. Ask separately what was indexed, what was retrieved, and what the generator received.

scenes.title: Four questions to take back to the library
scenes.claim: What text?   How large a unit?   What representation?   How grouped or expanded?
scenes.narration: Take four questions back to the library. What text was indexed? How large was each unit? How was it represented? How were matches grouped into results or expanded into context? A vector is a numerical object. A chunk is a searchable unit. Knowing both helps explain what a missing paper might really mean.
